paper_metadata.title: Reduction of Qubits in Quantum Algorithm for Monte Carlo Simulation by Pseudo-random Number Generator

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based quantum Monte Carlo method that reduces qubit requirements by generating pseudo‑random numbers sequentially on a quantum circuit and estimating averages via amplitude estimation. A proof-of-concept Qiskit simulation evaluates a 2‑variable integral with Nsamp = 8 using a 5‑bit LCG PRNG (period 30), producing a quantum estimate 0.078391 close to the sampled average 0.078394 (exact integral 0.074578). The claimed benefit is a theoretical quadratic speedup (O(N^{-1}) vs O(N^{-1/2})) while reducing qubit count through PRNG reuse.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo integration using a pseudo-random number generator on a gate-based quantum circuit, demonstrated on a 2-variable trigonometric integral with Qiskit simulation.

algorithm.variant: Amplitude estimation applied to Monte Carlo integration with PRNG-generated samples

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Pseudo-random numbers are generated sequentially on a quantum register; the integrand phase is encoded by controlled Ry rotations on an ancilla qubit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate I = (1/theta^Nvar) ∫_0^theta dx1 ... ∫_0^theta dx_Nvar sin^2(sum_i x_i) using Monte Carlo sampling and amplitude estimation.

problem_instance.description: Demonstration integral of a trigonometric function with phase depending on two variables.

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic integral with theta = pi/6 and Nvar = 2; 8 sample points generated from a 5-bit LCG sequence of period 30.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: PRN values xi are mapped to grid points (xi + 1/2)/2^r; sample points are formed by taking consecutive PRN subsequences.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compared exact integral value, exact average over sampled points, and quantum-simulator estimate; Qiskit simulation with amplitude-estimation likelihood procedure.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: LCG-based PRNG with parameters a=11, c=0, m=31, seed=1; 8 sample points; amplitude estimation via likelihood maximization.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate theta_a as the maximum point of the likelihood function from repeated measurements for m_k values.

speedup_claims.conditions: when amplitude estimation is used to estimate the sampled average Esamp; error scales as O(N_orac^-1) versus O(N_orac^-1/2) classically
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper presents a proof-of-concept simulator demonstration, but the quadratic speedup is a theoretical claim; the demonstrated example is too small-scale to establish empirical speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(N_orac) for amplitude estimation; overall error scales as O(N_samp^{-1/2} + N_orac^{-1})
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(N_orac^2) for classical Monte Carlo error scaling

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not estimated in the paper; advantage would require very large Nsamp and deep circuits due to sequential PRNG generation.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Large fault‑tolerant gate-based quantum computer capable of deep circuits proportional to the number of random variables (Nran). For finance use cases like credit portfolios with O(10^6) obligors, circuits would require extremely large logical qubit counts and very deep arithmetic circuits for PRNG, comparisons, and arithmetic.
limiting_factors: Only a noiseless simulator proof-of-concept is demonstrated
Circuit depth grows linearly with the number of random variables when using sequential PRNG generation
Arithmetic-heavy circuits (modular multiplication, comparisons, trigonometric functions) dominate cost
Quadratic speedup from amplitude estimation is likely negated by fault-tolerant overhead
Demonstration uses a tiny toy problem (2 variables, 8 samples)
